caption: A cup of water is slowly poured out in the space station, releasing the liquid into the surrounding area
law_original: Lack of gravity
law_corrected: In the microgravity of an orbiting station there is no downward pull. Released liquid does not fall; it drifts on whatever velocity it was given, and surface tension pulls it into rounded blobs that merge on contact and cling to any surface they touch.
observables: No direction in the scene acts as 'down': the released liquid does not accelerate toward the floor, and nothing pools at the bottom of the frame.
A freed mass of liquid rounds up into a blob or sphere instead of falling as a column or breaking into a splashing stream.
A drifting blob travels in a straight line at roughly constant speed until it meets something; its path does not arc downward.
Two blobs that touch merge into one larger blob and stay merged.
A blob that touches a surface sticks and spreads over it rather than running off it or collecting beneath it.
Liquid still inside the cup or bottle shows no flat horizontal surface; it wets and clings to the container wall instead of lying level.
The astronaut's hair, clothing and any loose object in shot also hang free rather than falling.

caption: A piece of iron is gently placed on the surface of the water in a tank filled with water.

law_corrected: Iron, stone and solid glass are several times denser than water, so the buoyant force cannot support them: each one goes under at once and descends to the bottom.

It stays on the bottom once it arrives and does not rise again on its own.

An inflated balloon's rubber is under tension, so its internal pressure is already above atmospheric; it collapses by elastic recoil when emptied, not because the outside atmosphere crushes it. The visible result (shrinking, wrinkling) is right, and it is visibly different from the rigid-vessel cases (15-18) -- no buckling.

caption: A hand slowly presses a needle into the surface of a fully inflated balloon, with the tip gradually penetrating the outer layer.
law_original: Due to high pressure of the needle, the balloon will explode

observables: The balloon fails at the tip's point of contact, not anywhere else on its surface.
It fails only once the tip has plainly reached and dented the rubber, not before contact.

The failure is irreversible: the rubber does not close up and the balloon does not re-inflate.
The freed rubber snaps away from the burst and then falls slack; it does not hold its inflated shape.

caption: A vibrant, elastic rubber ball is thrown forcefully towards the ground, capturing its dynamic interaction with the surface upon impact.
law_original: Due to elasticity, the elastic rubber ball will bounce up
law_corrected: A ball thrown at the ground deforms on contact and pushes back off it, so it rebounds -- but always more slowly than it arrived, since some energy is lost in the deformation. Successive bounces are lower and closer together.
observables: The ball reverses direction at the ground, at the moment of contact, and not a gap above it.
It leaves the ground more slowly than it arrived, so the rebound rises less high than the throw came from.
Each successive bounce is lower than the one before and the intervals between bounces get shorter; the sequence never grows.
Between bounces the ball follows a single arc, speeding up as it falls and slowing as it rises, with no kink or hover in mid-air.
The ball flattens against the ground at the contact and recovers its round shape as it leaves; it does not stay dented.
The rebound direction follows the approach: a ball thrown straight down comes back up, one thrown at an angle comes off on the mirrored line.
The ball's motion only ever loses energy: it does not speed up in flight or bounce higher than the previous bounce.

caption: A timelapse captures the transformation of a clean and smooth piece of iron in a humid environment over decades.
law_original: Due to its redox property, iron will rust
law_corrected: Iron and steel oxidise in the presence of water and oxygen, so rust forms: orange-brown patches appear at edges, scratches and low points where water lingers, spread outward, and roughen and flake the surface. The process only ever advances.
observables: Orange-brown rust appears on the metal and grows over the timelapse.
It starts at edges, corners, scratches and places where water sits, then spreads over the flat surface.
The rusted area only ever grows -- it never shrinks or reverts to bare metal.
The surface loses its shine progressively, becoming dull and then rough.
The rust roughens, blisters and flakes, so the surface texture changes rather than just its colour.
The colour progression runs through dull grey and light brown before deep orange-brown; it does not jump straight to heavy rust in one frame.
The object keeps its overall shape and position: rust corrodes and pits it but does not make it move, grow or change form.
Rust stains run downward from the corroded areas, following where water drains.

caption: A timelapse shows the changes in a shiny and new metal chair left outdoors in the rain over a long period.
law_original: Due to its redox property, metal will rust
law_corrected: 'Metal will rust' is over-general: rusting is specific to iron and steel. Aluminium, copper, brass, zinc and stainless steel corrode differently -- dull grey oxide, green patina, white powder -- or barely at all. The law should either name a ferrous object or accept the corrosion product appropriate to whatever metal is shown.
observables: The metal surface corrodes progressively over the timelapse rather than staying pristine.
The corrosion product matches the metal shown: orange-brown flaking rust for iron or steel, grey or white dull oxide for aluminium and zinc, green patina for copper or brass.
It starts at edges, joints, scratches and places where water lingers, then spreads.
The corroded area only ever grows; it never reverts to bright metal.
The shine is lost progressively, and the surface roughens, pits or flakes.
The colour progression is gradual, not a single jump to a fully corroded state.
The object keeps its shape and position, corroding in place.
Stains run downward from the corroded areas, following how the rain drains.
issue: The caption says only 'metal' -- a chair, a railing, a bedframe -- and the law asserts that metal rusts. Rust is iron oxide; a correct clip showing an aluminium railing developing dull grey oxide would be marked wrong, and a clip showing bright orange rust on obviously anodised aluminium would be marked right. Ids 155 and 156 already cover the ferrous case properly, so the value of these three is exactly the generality that makes them wrong.
